name: Rosa Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Kowal and Sons, a small roofing and renovation firm, five of us plus old Mr Kowal who still comes out to point at things. Mostly I'm up on roofs, replacing rotten rafters, battens, fascia boards, sometimes building a dormer, that's the little box window that sticks out of a roof. I'm in the van by seven, we pick up timber from the merchant on Station Road and we're on the job by eight. I like being up high on a clear morning, you can see the whole town. I hate wet slate and the end of a February day when your fingers don't work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven years, since my apprenticeship finished. I live with my boyfriend Dan, he drives a delivery van, so we're both out early and both worn out by nine at night. The pay's lower than the big roofing outfits in the city, but there aren't many roofing jobs in a town this size, so you don't leave a decent boss. We've got about two weeks' money saved, maybe. I don't use any of that AI stuff, I barely use my email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sounds about right. Every year there's something that's going to change everything, and the rain still gets in the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, honestly. If someone brought it up at the merchant's I'd say I never thought a computer was going to fix a roof anyway. I'm not online much, Dan does the posting in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's fine, which is the main thing. I'd still be on low pay and still have a bad shoulder by forty, but that was always the deal. I'd rather have a known problem than an unknown one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep going at Kowal's, try to put a bit by when the summer work's busy, and maybe ask for a small raise when Mr Kowal's son takes over properly. I'm not one for big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, though I wasn't that worried in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather have a known problem than an unknown one. What's the known problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, and my body. Roofers don't last, everyone knows that. Mr Kowal's knees are shot and he's seventy. That's my future and I've made my peace with it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything AI might do here, even in the small way the card says?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office side. Mrs Kowal does the quotes on paper with a calculator and it takes her a whole evening. If a computer did that faster, good for her. It wouldn't touch me.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much; if it came up at the timber merchant's I'd say I never thought a computer would fix a roof. Dan does the posting online in our house.
S0.think: Privately it means my job's fine, which is what matters most. I'd still have low pay and a bad shoulder by forty, but that was always the deal, and a known problem beats an unknown one.
S0.do: Keeps working at Kowal and Sons, tries to put money aside in the busy summer months, and asks for a small raise when the owner's son takes over.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit relieved, though she wasn't very worried to begin with.
S0.quote: I'd rather have a known problem than an unknown one.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is dry and low-key, and doesn't treat AI as part of her world at all. She has already accepted the physical cost of roofing as the price of a steady job. Her loyalty to a small local firm comes from having few other options in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one I don't like as much. Some jobs shrink, it says. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it depends on the job, and that people shouldn't panic. I'd say something like, they'll always need someone on a roof, which is what everyone in the trade says. I wouldn't get into politics about it, both sides just use these things to shout at each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not sure we're as safe as we say. The big firms have drones now that survey a roof in ten minutes, and Mrs Kowal said one of them quoted half our price on a job last spring. If the quoting and the surveying go to machines, a small firm like ours either keeps up or gets undercut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see, honestly, and keep working. If Kowal's bought a drone or a tablet I'd let the younger lad, Marek, do it. I'd try to save a little more, maybe skip our holiday to the coast this year, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it'd be in the back of my mind every time I saw a van from a bigger firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Marek do the new stuff. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be slow and I'd hate it, and he'd be fast and love it. That's not me being lazy, it's just being honest about what I'm good at. I'm good at timber and heights, not screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dan say to each other about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan would be more worried than me, because it's his van they'd replace first, isn't it, self-driving delivery. I'd tell him not to read the news before bed. We'd probably argue about whether to cancel the holiday.

S1.say: I'd say it depends on the job and people shouldn't panic, and that they'll always need someone on a roof. I wouldn't get into politics, because both sides just use it to shout at each other.
S1.think: Privately I'm not sure we're as safe as we say, since big firms already use drones to survey roofs and undercut our quotes. A small firm like Kowal's either keeps up or gets undercut.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what happens, leaving any new drone or tablet to a younger colleague. Saves a little more, possibly skipping this year's holiday to the coast.
S1.feel: Uneasy in the background, especially when she sees a bigger firm's van.
S1.quote: I'm good at timber and heights, not screens.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa's public line is the trade's comfort phrase, but privately she has already seen drones undercut her firm. She is clear-eyed that she wouldn't learn the new tools herself. Her partner's delivery job feels more exposed to her than her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots on roofs by 2028. I don't even know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say anything at first, I'd just listen to everyone else. If I did say something, it'd be that the government and the companies both let this happen without a plan. I don't trust either lot, never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be finished, and so would Dan. We'd both be doing the exact jobs a robot and a self-driving van would do. Two weeks of savings, rent due on the first, and nothing in this town but a supermarket that'd have robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but food and rent the same week. If Kowal's let me go, I'd ask my mum if Dan and I could move into her spare room, she's in a village about an hour away. I'd take any help that was going, benefits, food bank, whatever, and I'd look for any job that's still done by people, cleaning, care work, I don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. My stomach went when you said hands-on work. I keep thinking that was our safe bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Kowal and Sons in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Kowal would sell up, I think, or shut it. He's seventy, he wouldn't buy robots. His son might try. Either way it wouldn't be five of us anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent's due on the first. What's the first bill that goes unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance, probably, because we'd stop driving. Then the phone. Rent we'd pay until we couldn't, and then we'd go to Mum's. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

S2.say: At first I'd say nothing and just listen. If I said anything it would be that the government and the companies both let this happen without a plan, because I don't trust either lot.
S2.think: Privately I'd be finished, and so would Dan, because our jobs are exactly what robots and self-driving vans would do. With two weeks of savings and few jobs in town, there'd be nothing to fall back on.
S2.do: Cuts spending to food and rent the same week and plans to move into her mum's spare room with Dan if she's let go. Takes any help on offer and looks for any job still done by people.
S2.feel: Panicked, because hands-on work was supposed to be the safe bet.
S2.quote: My stomach went when you said hands-on work. I keep thinking that was our safe bet.
S2.fieldNote: This picture breaks Rosa's main source of calm, the belief that hands-on work is safe. Her household has two exposed jobs and almost no savings, and she sees no options locally. She blames government and companies equally rather than taking a side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Still fast. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better use the time, and that I hope the people in charge actually do something for once. I'd say it in a tired voice, because I'd be saying it about politicians who never do. I'd not be marching, I'm not the type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I'd probably get two or three more seasons on the roofs before it bites. That's something. But I know myself, I'd hope it went away rather than doing anything, because I'm bad at change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting money aside properly, maybe a hundred a month in a separate account so I don't touch it. I'd cut the takeaways and Dan's gaming subscription. I'd keep going at Kowal's and wait to see if the robots actually show up round here before I did anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Five years sounds like a lot until you think about how fast seven went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see if the robots show up round here. What would you need to see to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot on a roof in this town. Or Mr Kowal telling me he's thinking of buying one. Until then it's news, and news is mostly noise. I know that's probably too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mr Kowal's son if he asked you to learn to run one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, because I'd need the job. I'd be terrible at it at first and I'd moan. But if it's that or nothing, I'd learn.

S3.say: I'd say we'd better use the time and hope the people in charge do something for once, though I'd say it tiredly. I wouldn't march, I'm not the type.
S3.think: Privately five years means two or three more seasons on the roofs before it bites. But I'd hope it went away rather than act, because I'm bad at change.
S3.do: Puts about a hundred a month into a separate savings account and cuts takeaways and subscriptions. Keeps working at Kowal's and waits to see robots locally before doing anything bigger.
S3.feel: Alarmed, because five years sounds long until she remembers how fast the last seven went.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like a lot until you think about how fast seven went.
S3.fieldNote: Rosa knows her own pattern: she waits for proof on her doorstep and admits that may be too late. Still, she'd learn a new machine if the choice were that or nothing. The extra time eases her money panic only a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long way off for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the country to sort itself out, if it bothers. I'd say it to Dan, mainly, and maybe at Mum's on a Sunday. I'd tell people not to panic, because I think a lot of the talk would be overblown at the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable. I'd get most of my roofing life in before it hits, and my shoulder probably wouldn't last much past thirty-seven anyway. The bit that scares me is what comes after, because I don't have a second thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Kowal's and save steadily, try to get to three months' money. Maybe in year five or six I'd look at a forklift or crane licence, something with a machine, because I'd see which way it was going by then. I wouldn't do anything in the first year except save, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A slow, background anxious, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't have a second thing you're good at. What would you want it to be, if you could pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like dogs. I've always said I'd do dog walking or work at a kennel. That's not a career, though, is it. Dan laughs at me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what does the extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything and nothing. With two years we're in Mum's spare room. With ten I've probably got a bit saved and I've had my roofing years. But I still end up looking for something to do at thirty-seven.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time for the country to sort itself out if it bothers. I'd tell Dan and my family not to panic, because a lot of the early talk would be overblown.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels survivable, since I'd get most of my roofing years in before it hits. What scares me is after, because I don't have a second thing I'm good at.
S4.do: Keeps working at Kowal's and saves steadily towards three months of money. Waits until year five or six before considering a forklift or crane licence.
S4.feel: A slow, background anxiety that doesn't go away.
S4.quote: I still end up looking for something to do at thirty-seven.
S4.fieldNote: For Rosa, ten years mainly protects her savings and her remaining roofing years, not her long-term future. She'd delay any retraining until the trend was obvious. Her half-joking wish to work with dogs shows how little she's pictured a second career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Me and Dan both out at once with nothing saved, that's the nightmare. What would help is someone telling us exactly what jobs are still going to exist, in plain words, and a bit of money to tide us over while we found one. Not speeches, just that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small firms. Everyone talks about big companies, but Kowal's is five people and a van. If they go, nobody writes about it. There's thousands of firms like that.

headlineQuote: Kowal's is five people and a van. If they go, nobody writes about it.
portrait: Rosa Petrov is a 27-year-old roofer at a five-person family roofing firm in a small town, living with her delivery-driver boyfriend Dan on about two weeks of savings. She doesn't use AI and says plainly she's good at timber and heights, not screens. She is calm about the plateau and quietly uneasy about drones undercutting her firm, then panics at AGI in two years because both her and Dan's jobs would go at once. With five or ten years she would save and wait for proof on her doorstep, knowing that may be too late.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Dan would both lose their jobs at once with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A plain answer about which jobs will still exist and some money to tide them over while they find one, not speeches.
